[Jae holding a violin and bow in a black-and-white portrait](<https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/assets/jae-violin.jpeg>)

82 JAE / MUSIC & PRODUCTION

### I learned to make music. Then I had to get people to hear it.

In February 2024, I began releasing my own music under the name **82 Jae**. I used FL Studio to produce tracks, DistroKid to distribute them, and every low-cost promotional channel I could think of to try to reach listeners.

I didn't have a label or a professional team. I was learning every stage of the process by doing it myself.

> “Creating a song and building a career around that song turned out to be two very different problems.”

### Four things I actually tried.

1. **Distribution without a label.** Produced tracks using FL Studio and distributed them through DistroKid.
2. **Consistency.** Released a new song every Friday for approximately two months.
3. **QR-code promotion.** Shared direct links to my music during in-person conversations and networking.
4. **Communities.** Shared releases through Discord servers, university music communities, and social platforms.

I shared this process publicly in a LinkedIn post, not as a proven formula, but as a record of the approaches I had tried.

### What the numbers actually showed.

- **193,068** — STREAMS

- **16,462** — LISTENERS

- **49** — FOLLOWERS

- **202** — PLAYLIST ADDS

- **125** — SAVES

- **Aug 30** — 2024 SNAPSHOT

[Spotify for Artists dashboard for February 1 to August 30, 2024, showing 193,068 streams, 16,462 listeners, 125 saves, 202 playlist adds, and 49 followers](<https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/assets/spotify-proof.webp>)

Source: personal Spotify for Artists screenshot, February 1–August 30, 2024. The broader milestone is described as approximately 200,000 streams.

### 49 followers made me ask a different question.

I was happy to reach nearly 200,000 streams. But the follower count made me curious about how discovery differs from loyalty. A stream is not the same as a fan, and a fan is not automatically a sustainable source of income.

Those numbers alone don't prove my conversion rate or explain why people listened. They were enough to give me a new question to investigate.

> How can independent artists turn discovery into relationships that last?

That question became one of the starting points for [Sibyl](<https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/project.html>), an early-stage exploration of AI-assisted music marketing.

### Making marketing useful for a real business.

In 2026, I began managing social content for my family's medical clinic, Miraeyeonhap Clinic, across Threads, Instagram, and Naver Blog.

- **258K** — THREADS VIEWS / 30 DAYS

During a 30-day period in July–August 2026, our Threads content accumulated approximately 258,000 views. Some patients later said they had found the clinic through online content, including searches related to hypertension and weight management.

## When technology meets reality.

Source page: https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/work/military.html

My service in the Republic of Korea Air Force taught me why trust, context, reliability, and human judgment matter as much as technical capability.

ROK AIR FORCE

KOREAN–ENGLISH INTERPRETATION

PEER SUPPORT

[Jae wearing his Republic of Korea Air Force uniform in front of flags](<https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/assets/jae-military.jpeg>)

ROK AIR FORCE / ENGLISH LINGUIST

### A different kind of education.

Since July 2025, I've been serving in the Republic of Korea Air Force as a Korean–English linguist and interpreter as part of mandatory military service.

My work has included translation and consecutive interpretation in support of routine coordination between South Korean and American Air Force personnel. I also completed the Air Force's 870th basic training class and served as a chapel choir conductor.

Unlike my creative projects, this work takes place inside a highly structured environment where precision and responsibility are essential.

### Tools don't eliminate the need for judgment.

Supporting bilingual coordination made me appreciate how much depends on accurate communication, shared context, and trust between people.

I also interpreted during a software update. Seeing existing technology introduced into a structured organization strengthened my interest in the practical work of adoption: helping people understand a tool, trust it, and use it in context.

I began asking whether secure, human-supervised tools could make specialized communication more reliable without compromising accountability. I don't have a working solution, and military environments rightly impose strict reliability and security requirements.

> In high-stakes settings, the best tool is not necessarily the most advanced. It is the one that can be trusted in context.

### Listening is operationally important, too.

- **~50** — AIRMEN IN MY PEER-SUPPORT GROUP

- **10+** — ONE-ON-ONE CONVERSATIONS

- **2026** — PEER SUPPORT APPOINTMENT

As an Onmaeum (peer-support) airman, I was assigned to support roughly 50 fellow service members and held more than ten individual conversations. The responsibility reinforced something I also saw in marketing: if you want to help people, start by listening carefully.

My responsibility was to listen, offer support, and connect people to appropriate professional resources when needed.

### What works on a demo may not work in the field.

I'm interested in whether robots could take on dangerous tasks. My service has made me much more aware of the gap between technological possibility and safe, responsible implementation.

A product may work technically yet still face barriers involving safety, certification, security, integration, training, and trust. I think important companies can be built by understanding those barriers rather than ignoring them.

The problems I have encountered make me want to learn from people who build and deploy these tools.

### Another question worth exploring.

> How can we responsibly bring better technology into environments where mistakes carry serious consequences?

My immediate product experiment focuses on music technology, where I can test ideas quickly with creators. But I also want to learn from people building safe tools for hazardous work and dependable human-machine coordination.

This overview focuses on my responsibilities and lessons learned. No operational documents are included.

## Sibyl . Less guessing. More making.

Source page: https://jae-kim-haa-portfolio.seong-jae-kim.chatgpt.site/project.html

A concept for an AI growth copilot that turns independent musicians' marketing questions into specific experiments they can actually try.

NOT LAUNCHED

PROTOTYPE PREVIEW

MUSIC × AI

### Artists don't need more dashboards. They need to know what to try next.

While producing music, I learned that making a song was only the first challenge. While experimenting with short-form content, I learned how unpredictable reach can be. Sibyl began as a question: **could an assistant help independent artists choose and evaluate marketing experiments?**

Rather than promising a full analytics platform, the first useful version might simply help an artist go from “I released a song” to “here are three actions I can test this week.”

> Hypothesis, not yet a validated product.

### What would make this real?

1. **Interview artists.** Find out how they currently decide what to post and whether the decision itself is painful.
2. **Do the work manually.** Deliver a few thoughtful weekly plans to five musicians without automating everything.
3. **Track repeated use.** Ask whether artists come back after trying the ideas, not merely whether they liked the demo.
4. **Charge only if useful.** Test willingness to pay after seeing meaningful repeat engagement.

### Where it stands.

Sibyl is at the concept stage. This demo shows a possible workflow; live trend data and AI recommendations would require further development. User demand and willingness to pay still need to be tested.

My starting point is firsthand experience making music, reaching audiences, and understanding how frustrating promotion can feel. The next step is learning whether that insight maps to a product musicians want to use.
